newsitem.title: JAPAN: Consumers said to hold key to Japan economy.
newsitem.headline: Consumers said to hold key to Japan economy.

text.p: Consumers will hold the key to Japan's economic strength in the next business year after tax increases take money out of their pockets and make goods more expensive, analysts said in a Reuters poll released on Thursday.

The economists said they expect a slowdown in growth as the government seeks to rein in fiscal spending by ending special income tax cuts, raising the sales tax and alloting modest sums for public works.

The forecasts from 36 institutions produced an average of 1.5 percent real growth in gross domestic product (GDP) for fiscal 1997/98, down from the average forecast of 2.5 percent growth for the current year.
Forecasts for the next business year ranged from a low of 0.7 percent growth to a high of 2.5 percent.

"The sales tax rise and the end of special income tax cuts are the worry. Consumption is recovering slowly now but there'll be a big drop after April," said Yozo Nishimura, an economist at the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
The sales tax will be lifted to five percent from three percent. Both tax measures go into effect on April 1, the start of the fiscal year.
The survey covered 37 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.

The economists said empty pockets after spending sprees -- in particular, a rush for larger purchases such as cars and houses -- ahead of the sales tax rise, would result in the economy contracting somewhat during the April-June quarter.
But they also expected spending to gradually pick up later in the year. Capital expenditures, the main engine of growth in the current business year, were also expected to continue to lend support.

Some saw the consumption problem being exacerbated by a stagnant employment market. Core wages were unlikely to rise and overtime payments were likely to fall after companies reduce production in anticipation of weaker spending, they said.

"The unemployment rate is going to remain around 3.3 percent, which is high for Japan. Consumption will have a difficult time getting off the ground. On top of that, tax rises -- a double whammy," said Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan.

Among the more bearish of the forecasters, he predicted real GDP growth would rise by just 0.8 percent. Ushikubo added that industrial output was also likely to suffer as some industries, such as chemicals and pulp and paper, had not done enough to cut back on inventories.
Others were more optimistic, citing recent economic data supporting increasing firmness in Japan's still young economic recovery.
"The statistics have been very good, nothing to be ashamed of," said Michael Hartnett, chief economist at Merrill Lynch.
Merrill Lynch sees a weaker yen helping exports to push up GDP growth to a high level of 2.5 percent for fiscal 1997/98.
"What differentiates us from the consensus is that we are looking for the yen to depreciate. We see the yen going to 125 yen versus the dollar over the course of 1997," said Harnett.
A combination of a weak yen with interest rates at historic low levels and virtually no inflationary pressure would work to offset the effects of the tax rises, he said.
The survey was conducted between January 13 and 16.
